## Overview

This tutorial shows how to download, clean, and visualise long-term weather data for any airport in the world using the **NOAA Integrated Surface Database (ISD)** — no FTP, no API key, no paid data.

The example uses **Athens Eleftherios Venizelos (LGAV)**, but every step works for any ICAO station code.

**Outputs:**

| Plot | What it shows |
|------|--------------|
| Daily ribbon | Temperature range (min–max) for every day |
| Monthly ribbon | Smoothed monthly range with gradient line |
| Heatmap max | Monthly max temperature by year |
| Heatmap min | Monthly min temperature by year |
| Decomposition | Trend + seasonal + residual components |

---

## Packages

```{r packages}
library(rnoaa)
library(plotly)
```

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
# remotes::install_github("ropensci/rnoaa")   # use the GitHub version
# install.packages("plotly")
```

---

## 1. Find the station

NOAA ISD identifies stations by **USAF** and **WBAN** codes. The easiest way to find them is by ICAO airport code.

```{r station}
stations<-isd_stations(refresh=FALSE)

# explore Greek stations
stations[stations$ctry%in%"GR",c("station_name","icao","usaf","wban","lat","lon")]
```

```{r lgav}
lgav<-stations[stations$icao%in%"LGAV",]
station<-lgav$station_name
usaf<-lgav$usaf[1]
wban<-lgav$wban[1]

message("Station : ",station)
message("USAF    : ",usaf,"   WBAN: ",wban)
message("Location: ",round(lgav$lat[1],3),"°N  ",round(lgav$lon[1],3),"°E")
```

> Change `"LGAV"` to any ICAO code — `"EGLL"` for Heathrow, `"KJFK"` for New York, etc.

---

## 2. Download hourly ISD data

`rnoaa::isd()` replaces the old wget + FTP workflow. It downloads, decompresses, and parses the ISD binary format automatically. Each call fetches one year; a loop collects all years into a list.

```{r download}
years<-2001:2026
data_list<-list()

for(yr in years) {
  tryCatch({
    d<-rnoaa::isd(usaf=usaf,wban=wban,year=yr,progress=FALSE)
    data_list[[as.character(yr)]]<-d
    message("  downloaded ",yr," (",nrow(d)," rows)")
  },error=function(e) message("  skip ",yr,": ",conditionMessage(e)))
}

# the years do not all have the same columns: give each year every column, NA where it has none
columns<-unique(unlist(lapply(data_list,names)))
data_list<-lapply(data_list,function(d) {
  d<-as.data.frame(d)
  d[setdiff(columns,names(d))]<-NA
  d[columns]
})
df_raw<-do.call(rbind,data_list)
rownames(df_raw)<-NULL
message("Total rows: ",nrow(df_raw))
```

> Years where data are unavailable are silently skipped by `tryCatch`. 2026 data may be partial depending on when you run this.

---

## 3. Clean: sentinel values and date parsing

### Why sentinel values matter

NOAA ISD encodes missing measurements as **9999** in the raw file. After dividing by 10 (ISD stores all values as tenths of the unit), missing temperature becomes **999.9°C** — a physically impossible value that will corrupt any aggregate (mean, max, min) if not removed.

```{r clean}
df_data<-df_raw
df_data$date<-as.Date(df_data$date,format="%Y%m%d") # isd() returns "YYYYMMDD" strings
df_data$temp<-as.numeric(df_data$temperature)/10
df_data$dew<-as.numeric(df_data$temperature_dewpoint)/10
df_data$wind_spd<-as.numeric(df_data$wind_speed)/10
df_data$slp<-as.numeric(df_data$air_pressure)/10
for(k in c("temp","dew","wind_spd","slp")) {
  df_data[[k]]<-ifelse(df_data[[k]]>900|df_data[[k]]< -200,NA,df_data[[k]])
}
df_data<-df_data[!is.na(df_data$date),]

df_data[df_data==999.9]<-NA # catch any remaining sentinels
df_data$month<-sub("-\\d{2}$","",df_data$date) # "YYYY-MM" column
```

**Two-pass sentinel removal:**

1. `ifelse(x>900|x< -200,NA,x)`, for each of the four measures — catches the scaled sentinels immediately after division
2. `df_data[df_data == 999.9] <- NA` — safety net for any that slipped through

---

## 4. Daily and monthly aggregates

`aggregate()` applies a function (here `max` or `min`) to every numeric column, grouped by date or month. Columns are then renamed with `_max` / `_min` suffixes before merging.

```{r aggregate}
measures<-names(df_data)[sapply(df_data,is.numeric)]
daily_max<-aggregate(df_data[measures],list(date=df_data$date),max,na.rm=TRUE)
daily_min<-aggregate(df_data[measures],list(date=df_data$date),min,na.rm=TRUE)
month_max<-aggregate(df_data[measures],list(month=df_data$month),max,na.rm=TRUE)
month_min<-aggregate(df_data[measures],list(month=df_data$month),min,na.rm=TRUE)

names(daily_max)[-1]<-paste0(names(daily_max)[-1],"_max")
names(daily_min)[-1]<-paste0(names(daily_min)[-1],"_min")
names(month_max)[-1]<-paste0(names(month_max)[-1],"_max")
names(month_min)[-1]<-paste0(names(month_min)[-1],"_min")

daily<-merge(daily_max,daily_min)
month<-merge(month_max,month_min)

daily$date<-as.Date(daily$date)
month$month_date<-as.Date(paste0(month$month,"-01"))
month<-month[order(month$month_date),]
```

```{r aggregate_preview}
head(daily[,c("date","temp_max","temp_min","wind_spd_max")],6)
```

---

## 5. Plots

The charts share their colours, a dashed line at 0 °C, a time axis with one tick a year, and a helper that adds the title and the source:

```{r chart_style}
# from cold (blue) to hot (red), for the highest temperatures
temp_colors<-c("#2166ac","#74add1","#fee090","#f46d43","#a50026")
temp_scale<-lapply(seq_along(temp_colors),
                   function(i) list((i-1)/(length(temp_colors)-1),temp_colors[i]))
# a dashed line at 0 °C, and a time axis with one tick a year
zero_line<-list(type="line",xref="paper",x0=0,x1=1,y0=0,y1=0,
                line=list(color="white",width=1,dash="dash"))
years_axis<-list(tickformat="%Y",dtick="M12",tickangle=-90)

# the title of a chart, its source as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,y_title="",x_axis=list(),y_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                note_y=-0.14,...) {
  note<-list(text="Source: NOAA ISD via rnoaa",xref="paper",yref="paper",x=1,y=note_y,
             xanchor="right",yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=10,color="#7F7F7F"))
  result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left"),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
# the titles of panels stacked one above the other, each above its panel
panel_titles<-function(p,titles) {
  domains<-plotly_build(p)$x$layout
  axes<-c("yaxis",paste0("yaxis",seq_along(titles)[-1]))
  result<-lapply(seq_along(titles),function(k) {
    list(text=paste0("<b>",titles[k],"</b>"),x=0,xref="paper",xanchor="left",
         y=domains[[axes[k]]]$domain[2],yref="paper",yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE,
         font=list(size=12))
  })
  return(result)
}
```

### Daily temperature ribbon

Each day is a bar from its lowest to its highest temperature (a plotly bar with a `base`), and the bars side by side form a band. The colour of each bar is mapped to `temp_max` through a diverging scale — cold days are blue, hot days are red.

```{r plot_daily, fig.width = 10}
# each day a bar from its lowest to its highest temperature, coloured by the highest; alone: drawn
# on its own, with its colour scale
daily_bars<-function(alone=TRUE) {
  result<-plot_ly(daily,x=~date,y=~round(temp_max-temp_min,1),base=~temp_min,type="bar",
                  marker=list(color=~temp_max,colorscale=temp_scale,showscale=alone,opacity=0.7,
                              colorbar=list(title="Max °C")),
                  text=~paste0(format(date,"%d %b %Y"),": ",temp_min," to ",temp_max," °C"),
                  hoverinfo="text",textposition="none") %>%
    layout(bargap=0,xaxis=years_axis,yaxis=list(zeroline=FALSE),shapes=list(zero_line))
  return(result)
}

daily_bars() %>%
  chart(paste0(str_aes(station),"<br><sup>Daily temperature range</sup>"),
        y_title="Temperature (°C)")
```

### Monthly ribbon

Aggregating to monthly level removes the noise and makes the seasonal pattern clearer. The max temperature gets points coloured on the same scale; the min stays a white line.

```{r plot_monthly, fig.width = 10}
# the range of each month, its highest temperature as points coloured like the days, and its lowest
monthly_band<-function(alone=TRUE) {
  result<-plot_ly(month,x=~month_date) %>%
    add_ribbons(ymin=~temp_min,ymax=~temp_max,fillcolor=toRGB("#74add1",0.45),line=list(width=0),
                hoverinfo="skip") %>%
    add_lines(y=~temp_max,line=list(color="#9e9e9e",width=1),hoverinfo="skip") %>%
    add_markers(y=~temp_max,
                marker=list(color=~temp_max,colorscale=temp_scale,showscale=alone,size=6,
                            colorbar=list(title="Max °C")),
                text=~paste0(format(month_date,"%b %Y"),": highest ",temp_max," °C"),
                hoverinfo="text") %>%
    add_lines(y=~temp_min,line=list(color="white",width=1.5),
              text=~paste0(format(month_date,"%b %Y"),": lowest ",temp_min," °C"),
              hoverinfo="text") %>%
    layout(showlegend=FALSE,xaxis=years_axis,yaxis=list(zeroline=FALSE),shapes=list(zero_line))
  return(result)
}

monthly_band() %>%
  chart(paste0(str_aes(station),"<br><sup>Monthly temperature range</sup>"),
        y_title="Temperature (°C)")
```

### Heatmaps

A calendar heatmap puts **year on the x-axis** and **month on the y-axis**, with temperature encoded as fill colour. This format is ideal for spotting anomalies — an unusually hot August or a cold February stands out immediately.

```{r heatmaps, fig.width = 10}
month$year<-substr(month$month,1,4)
month$mon<-substr(month$month,6,7)

# one measure as a calendar: years across, months up, the median of all months in the light middle
# colour; alone: drawn on its own, with its colour scale and the value in each cell
heat_panel<-function(column,alone=TRUE) {
  z<-month[[column]]
  middle<-(median(z)-min(z))/(max(z)-min(z))
  result<-plot_ly(month,x=~year,y=~mon,z=z,type="heatmap",
                  colorscale=list(list(0,"#256abf"),list(middle,"#f0efec"),list(1,"#e34948")),
                  showscale=alone,xgap=1,ygap=1,text=paste0(round(z,1),"°C"),
                  texttemplate=if(alone) "%{text}" else "",textfont=list(size=9,color="#333333"),
                  hovertemplate="%{x}-%{y}: %{text}<extra></extra>",colorbar=list(title="°C")) %>%
    layout(xaxis=list(type="category",tickangle=-90),
           yaxis=list(type="category",categoryorder="array",categoryarray=sprintf("%02d",1:12)))
  return(result)
}

heat_panel("temp_max") %>% chart("Monthly Max Temperature",note_y=-0.16)
heat_panel("temp_min") %>% chart("Monthly Min Temperature",note_y=-0.16)
```

### All four together

```{r multiplot, fig.height = 14, fig.width = 10}
# the four charts one above the other; their colour scales and values are in the charts above
together<-subplot(daily_bars(FALSE),monthly_band(FALSE),heat_panel("temp_max",FALSE),
                  heat_panel("temp_min",FALSE),nrows=4,margin=0.035)
titles<-c("Daily temperature range","Monthly temperature range","Monthly max temperature",
          "Monthly min temperature")
together %>%
  chart(str_aes(station),annotations=panel_titles(together,titles),showlegend=FALSE,note_y=-0.03,
        margin=list(t=70,b=50))
```

---

## 6. Seasonal decomposition

`decompose()` splits a time series into three additive components:

- **Trend** — the long-term direction (is the station getting warmer?)
- **Seasonal** — the repeating annual cycle (summer peaks, winter troughs)
- **Random** — what's left after removing trend and seasonal (unusual events, measurement noise)

The `frequency = 365` tells R the series repeats annually. The day of the year of the first date (`format(first_day,"%j")`) sets the correct starting position within the first year.

```{r decomp, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}
first_day<-min(daily$date)
ts_temp<-ts(daily$temp_max,frequency=365,
            start=c(as.numeric(format(first_day,"%Y")),as.numeric(format(first_day,"%j"))))

fit<-decompose(ts_temp)

# the series and its three components, by date
components<-data.frame(date=daily$date,
                       Data=as.numeric(fit$x),
                       Trend=as.numeric(fit$trend),
                       Seasonal=as.numeric(fit$seasonal),
                       Random=as.numeric(fit$random))
components[-1]<-round(components[-1],2)
# one panel each; style() keeps one hover text for the whole line (given to plot_ly(), it would be
# repeated for every day)
panels<-lapply(names(components)[-1],function(k) {
  plot_ly(components,x=~date,y=reformulate(k),type="scatter",mode="lines",
          line=list(color="#404040",width=0.7)) %>%
    style(hovertemplate=paste0(k,", %{x|%d %b %Y}: %{y:.1f} °C<extra></extra>"))
})
decomposition<-subplot(panels,nrows=4,shareX=TRUE,margin=0.04)
decomposition %>%
  chart(paste0("Seasonal decomposition<br><sup>",str_aes(station),", daily max</sup>"),
        x_axis=years_axis,annotations=panel_titles(decomposition,names(components)[-1]),
        showlegend=FALSE,note_y=-0.08,margin=list(t=95))
```

> **Reading the decomposition:** If the trend panel slopes upward over 20+ years, that is a local warming signal. The random panel should look like white noise — large spikes indicate extreme weather events.

---

## Adapting to another airport

Change only these two lines and re-run everything:

```{r other_station, eval=FALSE}
lgav<-stations[stations$icao%in%"EGLL",] # London Heathrow
years<-2000:2026
```

Any ICAO code in the ISD station list will work. To search by country:

```{r search, eval=FALSE}
stations[stations$ctry%in%"UK",c("station_name","icao","usaf","wban")]
```
